== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: No information / Can't tell (single-wave cross-sectional data collection in May-June 2013; complete item data for all 294 interviewed customers in price and expenditure ANOVAs [df = 2, 291] and 22 household water samples from every 13th respondent, but kiosk and customer refusal/non-response rates are not reported and kiosk sample totals are internally inconsistent: 90 stated vs 97 summed across strata vs 103 implied by F(2, 100))
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk of bias (only two non-randomly targeted DMM slums, which also received external French donor capital investment and WSP technical assistance, are compared post-intervention to a single adjacent control slum via unadjusted one-way ANOVAs without pre-intervention baseline measurements, regression controls, or cluster-level adjustment)
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate institutional description (grounded in Kenya Water Act 2002, WASREB licensing, KIWASCO's bulk-supply master-operator vs direct-kiosk governance arrangements, and informal landlord-tenant lease restrictions, but operationalized strictly as a settlement-level binary indicator without coding formal DMM contracts, tariff schedules, or regulatory instruments)
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate risk of bias (microbiological E. coli and total coliform testing used objective laboratory membrane filtration, and per-20L kiosk price is salient, but monthly household water expenditure, 6-month supply reliability satisfaction, and service complaints relied on retrospective self-reports collected by unblinded local student interviewers, and kiosk observations coincided with a day-two main-line outage in DMM slums)
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Mixed quality (objective standard m-ColiBlue24 membrane-filtration laboratory assay for E. coli and total coliforms, though household subsample size was small [n = 22 total, n = 4 in control slum] and pooled across arms; economic and reliability outcomes relied on unvalidated self-reported monthly spending and a single binary 6-month satisfaction question)
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Serious risk of bias (no pre-analysis plan or pre-registered protocol; microbiological results for the 8 kiosk and 22 household samples are pooled rather than reported separately for DMM vs control slums despite water quality being a stated comparative outcome and basis for concluding DMM improved safe water access, and household water quantity consumed is listed as an evaluation dimension in Section 4 without comparative results)
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Serious risk of bias (community-group-managed kiosks [~5%] were excluded from the sampling frame; kiosk sample counts are inconsistent [90 stated vs 44+28+25 = 97 vs N = 103 in queue ANOVA]; and intercepting adult customers at operating utility kiosks post-intervention conditions on active kiosk patronage, excluding DMM households with private piped connections, households priced out to wells/vendors, and child water collectors)

domain_ratings.justification: Serious risk of bias. DMM was non-randomly implemented in Nyalenda A and B (Kisumu's largest slum, specifically selected for donor-backed upgrading) and evaluated via a single post-intervention cross-section (May-June 2013) against one adjacent non-DMM slum (Manyatta B). There are no pre-intervention baseline measures of tariffs, reliability, or water quality, and analyses rely solely on unadjusted one-way ANOVAs and percentages without multivariable control for household income, household size, tenure, network proximity, or settlement clustering (only an unquantified statement that respondent socio-demographics did not significantly differ).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Serious risk of bias. Sampling intercepted 3-5 adult customers (>18 years) actively buying water at operating individual KIWASCO kiosks post-intervention (excluding ~5% community-group-managed kiosks, households served by DMM private piped connections, residents relying solely on wells/springs/vendors due to cost or outages, and children fetching water, while oversampling frequent daytime kiosk users). Kiosk sample numbers are also internally inconsistent: Section 2.1 states 90 kiosks were sampled, stratum counts sum to 97 (44 + 28 + 25), and Section 3.1 queue/container ANOVAs report df = (2, 100), implying 103 observations. Household water testing included only 4 households in the Manyatta B control arm (out of 22 total).

Low risk of bias. Intervention status (DMM with metered master-operators in Nyalenda A and B versus direct utility-to-kiosk licensing without DMM in Manyatta B) was unambiguously defined at the settlement and utility-registry level prior to outcome data collection, using KIWASCO's administrative list of water kiosks.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Moderate risk of bias. Alongside DMM governance, Nyalenda A and B received targeted external co-interventions—funding from the French Embassy in Kenya, facilitation/technical assistance from WSP, and infrastructure expansion investment from the French Development Agency—that were not matched in Manyatta B, complicating attribution of lower prices and service differences purely to delegated management governance. Operational disruptions (including a main-line KIWASCO outage on day two of fieldwork in Nyalenda A and B and some operators selling shallow-well water during outages) reflect real-world service conditions under evaluation.

No information. Among the 294 interviewed customers (109 Nyalenda A, 107 Nyalenda B, 78 Manyatta B), the primary ANOVAs for 20-litre water price and monthly water expenditure have df = (2, 291), indicating zero item-level missingness among enrolled interviewees, and 22 household water samples were obtained from every 13th interviewee (floor(294/13) = 22). However, the paper reports no information on kiosk-level or customer-level refusal/non-response rates during recruitment, nor any explanation for the discrepancy between 90 stated kiosks, 97 summed stratum kiosks, and 103 df-implied observations in Section 3.1.

Moderate risk of bias. Microbiological water quality (total coliforms and E. coli via 24-hour m-ColiBlue24 membrane filtration) was assessed objectively in a laboratory, and current kiosk price per 20L jerrican is concrete, but monthly household water expenditure, 6-month satisfaction with water availability, alternative source reliance, and perceived kiosk challenges were collected via unblinded interviewer-administered questionnaires by local students familiar with the three slums, introducing recall and social desirability biases. Single-visit queue and container counts could also be affected by time-of-day and acute supply outages.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: Serious risk of bias. No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered study protocol is reported (only ethical review approvals). Critically, although Section 2.3 sampled household water across Nyalenda A (n = 10), Nyalenda B (n = 8), and Manyatta B (n = 4) and Section 4 states the study compared DMM and control slums on water quality and water quantity used, Section 3.7 and Table 1 pool all 8 kiosk and 22 household microbiological results without reporting contamination by settlement/intervention arm (while still claiming in Discussion that DMM improved access to safe water), and comparative water quantity data are omitted.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Nzengya (2018) is a non-randomized post-intervention comparative cross-sectional evaluation of KIWASCO's Delegated Management Model (DMM) in two informal settlements in Kisumu, Kenya (Nyalenda A and Nyalenda B) compared against an adjacent non-DMM 'control' slum (Manyatta B), combining customer-intercept questionnaires (n = 294), structured kiosk observations, and membrane-filtration microbiological water testing (n = 46 samples, including 22 household storage samples). Appraised with ROBINS-I, the study has an overall Serious risk of bias. Classification of settlement-level DMM status is Low risk (D3), and laboratory enumeration of E. coli and total coliforms used a valid standard assay, though unblinded interviewer-administered recall items for monthly water expenditure and 6-month reliability introduce Moderate measurement risk (D6) and co-occurring French donor infrastructure investments create Moderate co-intervention concerns (D4). However, internal validity is compromised by Serious confounding risk (D1: post-only comparison of two donor-targeted treated slums against one control slum using unadjusted one-way ANOVAs with no pre-intervention baseline or covariate/cluster controls), Serious participant-selection risk (D2: intercepting adult customers at active individual kiosks post-intervention conditions on kiosk patronage, excludes ~5% community-group kiosks and non-kiosk households, and exhibits inconsistent kiosk sample totals of 90 stated vs 97 summed vs 103 in ANOVA), No information on recruitment refusal rates (D5), and Serious selective/incomplete reporting (D7: pooling microbiological results across DMM and control slums in Table 1 and omitting comparative household water quantity figures despite claiming comparative evaluation on both dimensions).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Non-randomized post-intervention comparative cross-sectional study (controlled observational evaluation comparing two DMM intervention slums with an adjacent non-DMM control slum via kiosk customer-intercept surveys, structured kiosk observations, and microbiological water sampling)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Intervention background and institutional/legal context: PDF pp. 2-4 (Sections 1.1-1.3). Comparative 'control' slum design, sampling, ethics approvals, statistical analysis, and microbiological laboratory methods: PDF pp. 4-6 (Sections 1.3, 2, 2.1-2.3, Footnote 1). Empirical results and Table 1/Figures 2-3: PDF pp. 6-10 (Sections 3.1-3.7). Comparative claims and limitations in Discussion: PDF pp. 10-11 (Section 4).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I was selected because the study explicitly evaluates a municipal utility governance intervention—KIWASCO's Delegated Management Model (DMM) implemented in Nyalenda A and B—using an adjacent untreated settlement (Manyatta B) explicitly designated as a 'control' slum to identify impacts of DMM (PDF p. 4, Sections 1.3 and 2). JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies was ruled out because the study is structured as an explicit intervention-versus-control program evaluation rather than an associational cross-sectional survey without an intervention comparator. MMAT was ruled out because open-ended survey questions and kiosk observations were quantized into percentages and one-way ANOVAs without an independent qualitative analytical strand (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2).
